name: CodeSandbox
whyPeoplePay: CodeSandbox sells the machine you did not have to set up. A link opens a running development environment in seconds, a branch or a pull request gets its own copy, a template starts a project before you have installed anything, and the whole thing can be embedded in a document or handed to a stranger who has no toolchain at all. You are paying for provisioning, for the sandbox being disposable, and for somebody else keeping the VMs warm.

plans.name: Free
plans.note: 400 VM credits a month and a cap on how many sandboxes a workspace keeps.

plans.name: Pro
plans.note: $9 a month on the annual plan. A base allowance of 1,000 VM credits a month; more are bought as add-ons, so the bill moves with how long the machines stay awake.

pricing.note: codesandbox.io/pricing and the pricing pages under codesandbox.io/docs both answered our fetch with HTTP 403, so these figures were corroborated by search against CodeSandbox's own subscription and credit-usage documentation rather than read off the vendor page directly. Two things are genuinely uncertain: whether Pro is billed per workspace or per editor once a second person joins, and what a real monthly bill looks like once VM credit add-ons are counted, because credits are consumed by machine uptime rather than by seats. Re-check both against the live page before quoting a saving.

ranked.rationale: The closest thing to the editor half of CodeSandbox that you can run yourself: the same VS Code workbench, the same keybindings, the same terminal, reachable from any browser on a machine you control. What it does not reproduce is the part CodeSandbox actually charges for, which is a fresh disposable VM per branch and a link that boots one for someone else. This is one persistent environment that you maintain, and the honest trade is that you swap instant provisioning for never being metered.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Coder
evaluatedNotTested.note: The workspace manager from the same company, and the closer structural match to CodeSandbox: it provisions per-developer environments from Terraform templates, handles multiple users, and treats workspaces as things you create and destroy. It is also a platform rather than an install, with a control plane, a database and a provisioner to operate, so it belongs on a team's roadmap rather than in a one-command entry. AGPL-3.0, actively released.

evaluatedNotTested.name: OpenVSCode Server
evaluatedNotTested.note: Upstream VS Code with the web server switched on, tracking Microsoft's releases closely and still shipping, though at a slower cadence than code-server. The difference that decides it for a public hostname is authentication: their Docker image runs with --without-connection-token by default, which their README states plainly means anyone who reaches the host and port gets the IDE. You would be supplying the login layer yourself.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Gitpod Self-Hosted
evaluatedNotTested.note: The obvious CodeSandbox analogue on paper, and not a live option in practice. The repository is still worked on, but its releases stop at 2022.11.3 in June 2023, and there is nothing newer to install self-hosted. Listed so nobody spends an evening discovering that.
